claims.statement: [Evidence] Since 1 January 2026, EU importers above the 50-tonne mass threshold must obtain authorised-declarant status, buy CBAM certificates, declare embedded emissions, and surrender certificates annually; certificate prices track EU ETS auctions, and proven carbon prices paid in the country of production can be deducted.

[Evidence] The current consolidated regulation sets the first surrender deadline for 2026 imports at 30 September 2027, requires quarterly certificate coverage equal to at least 50% of embedded emissions from 2027, and imposes per-certificate penalties for shortfalls; unauthorised import above the threshold can attract a penalty three to five times the standard amount.

[Evidence] Actual-emissions declarations require independent verification by an accredited verifier, with the Commission expecting the first verifier accreditations around September 2026 and verification reports flowing from non-EU installations through the registry to declarants.

[Evidence] Corrected definitive-period defaults apply mark-ups of 10% in 2026, 20% in 2027, and 30% from 2028 for cement, iron and steel, aluminium, and hydrogen; fertiliser defaults carry a 1% mark-up.

[Inference] Where a supplier’s verified actual emissions are below the marked-up default, or where an eligible foreign carbon price can be proven, better evidence management can generate directly measurable certificate savings from which the product can charge.

[Inference] A partner-distributed evidence and liability layer can be more defensible than a filing-only tool because repeated supplier-installation records create reusable mappings, benchmarks, and workflow switching costs.

contrary_evidence: [Evidence, src-ec-definitive] The 50-tonne threshold excludes smaller importers, so the addressable market is substantially narrower than the population of all firms importing covered goods.
[Evidence, src-ec-verification] Software cannot replace regulated verification: actual-emissions claims depend on independent accredited verifiers and non-EU installation cooperation.
[Evidence, src-eurlex-cbam] The official CBAM Registry already handles core declarations and certificates, limiting willingness to pay for a thin reporting interface.
[Inference] A supplier with emissions above the applicable default may rationally prefer the default, eliminating the savings case.
[Inference] Customs, ERP, and ESG incumbents may bundle CBAM functionality and compress standalone pricing.

economics.acquisition_route: Inference: revenue-share referrals from customs brokers and accredited verifiers should be the primary scalable route; founder-led outreach to 30–50 Polish steel and aluminium importers can validate the first narrow workflow.
economics.capital_required_pln: Inference: 60000–100000 PLN for a secure MVP, specialist legal review, insurance, integration work, and 6–9 months of pilots; the company should never finance customers’ CBAM certificates.
economics.founder_net_worth_path: Inference: years 1–2 reach 10–25 Polish customers and roughly 0.5–1.5 million PLN ARR; years 3–5 expand through partners to 80–150 CEE customers at roughly 48000–72000 PLN ARR each, producing about 4–10 million PLN ARR. At 25–35% EBITDA and 60–80% retained ownership, cumulative retained earnings plus conservatively valued equity could plausibly exceed 5 million PLN in years 5–7, but customer count, pricing, margins, and valuation remain unvalidated.
economics.founder_time: Inference: 20–25 hours per week during validation, falling toward 10–15 hours after supplier outreach and verifier handoffs are delegated; this remains compatible with the founder’s stated daily limit but not if the service stays bespoke.
economics.gross_margin_basis: Inference: 70–85% gross margin after the workflow is productised; early pilots may be only 40–60% because supplier chasing, legal review, and exception handling remain manual.
economics.payback: Inference: structure pilots so the first-year fee is no more than 20–30% of documented certificate savings or avoided remediation cost, targeting customer payback inside six months; neither savings magnitude nor willingness to pay is yet validated.
economics.pricing: Inference: 12000–25000 PLN onboarding, 2500–8000 PLN per month based on import volume and supplier count, plus an optional 8–12% of independently documented certificate savings.
economics.retention_or_repeat: Evidence supports an annual declaration and certificate cycle with continuing monitoring and quarterly certificate-coverage requirements from 2027; inference is that ongoing imports, supplier changes, updated defaults, and evidence renewal can sustain monthly retention.

fingerprint.compounding_advantage: A permissioned graph linking CN codes, suppliers, production installations, evidence quality, verification outcomes, default-versus-actual emissions, and realised certificate costs can improve automation, supplier benchmarking, and switching costs with every reporting cycle.
fingerprint.customer: Polish and then CEE mid-market importers exceeding 50 tonnes per year of covered steel, aluminium, cement, fertiliser, or hydrogen goods, with finance, customs, or compliance staff currently coordinating supplier evidence manually.
fingerprint.distribution_mechanism: Partner-led acquisition through customs brokers, accredited CBAM verifiers, environmental consultancies, accounting firms, and sector associations, supplemented by targeted outbound to Polish importers near or above the threshold.
fingerprint.offer_and_business_model: Secure liability-calculation software bundled with supplier-evidence collection, exception handling, verifier handoff, foreign-carbon-price deduction support, and audit-ready exports; recurring SaaS plus managed-service and savings-share revenue.
fingerprint.payer_and_paid_event: The importer’s CFO, customs head, or compliance lead pays an onboarding fee, a monthly monitoring subscription while covered imports continue, and optionally a percentage of independently documented certificate savings.
fingerprint.problem_trigger: The definitive CBAM regime creates recurring emissions declarations and certificate purchases; default emissions for major sectors carry an escalating conservative mark-up, while using actual data requires verified evidence from non-EU installations.

founder_fit: Data-science and AI skills fit document extraction, emissions calculations, anomaly detection, liability forecasting, and workflow automation.
Finance-oriented thinking fits translating emissions evidence into cash exposure, working-capital forecasts, and measurable savings.
Polish and EU context supports a local-language wedge before expansion across CEE.

The family renewable-energy business can provide nearby industrial and customs-adjacent interviews, workflow observations, and potential channel introductions without requiring it to be the target customer.
A productised, partner-distributed model can start within roughly five hours per day and avoids dependence on a public-facing personal brand.
The initial capital need can fit within approximately 100000 PLN if regulated verification and legal opinions are purchased from partners rather than built in-house.
risks: Regulatory amendments could change scope, thresholds, mark-ups, deadlines, or calculation methods.
Incorrect calculations or missed deadlines could create material professional-liability exposure.
Customs and supplier emissions records are commercially sensitive and demand strong security controls.
Non-EU suppliers may refuse or fail to provide usable installation-level data.
The managed-service component could overwhelm the founder’s part-time capacity before automation is proven.
Enterprise trust requirements and procurement cycles may delay revenue beyond the available bootstrap runway.
Dependence on verifier partners could constrain delivery, margins, and customer ownership.
thesis: Inference: build a Polish-first software-plus-managed-service platform for mid-market importers above the CBAM mass threshold, initially in steel and aluminium. It would ingest customs and ERP records, forecast certificate liabilities, collect installation-level emissions evidence from non-EU suppliers, coordinate accredited verification, compare verified actual emissions with marked-up defaults, capture eligible foreign carbon-price deductions, and produce registry-ready records. The recurring subscription protects a mandatory certificate budget and compliance process; a savings-linked fee aligns payment with demonstrable reductions in certificate purchases.
title: CBAM Cost-Control Ledger for Polish and CEE Importers
uncertainties: The number and concentration of Polish and CEE importers above the threshold by sector are not established by the cited evidence.
The distribution of actual-versus-default emissions gaps, and therefore attainable certificate savings, is unknown.
Importer willingness to share customs data and pay a savings-linked fee is untested.
Registry integration and export capabilities may constrain automation.
Accredited-verifier capacity, pricing, and willingness to partner are not yet known.
It is unknown whether customs brokers will refer customers or treat the product as a competing service.
